title: Comparison of Two-Atom Cross Spectra in de Sitter Spacetime, Uniformly Accelerated Minkowski Vacuum, and a Thermal Bath
abstract: We study the weak coupling of two identical two-level atoms to a four-dimensional massless conformally coupled scalar field and compare three settings with the same local temperature but different physical origins: comoving atoms in the Bunch--Davies vacuum of de Sitter spacetime, transversely separated uniformly accelerated atoms in the Minkowski vacuum, and static atoms in a Minkowski thermal bath. We first derive the two-atom cross spectra in the three settings and then obtain the single-atom local spectra uniformly from the zero-separation limit. When $a=H$ and $β=2π/H$, the complete local Wightman kernels and local spectra are identical in all three cases. At finite separation, a genuine thermal bath produces a $\sinc(ΩL)$ spatial factor, whereas de Sitter spacetime and the transversely accelerated vacuum produce a hyperbolic geometric factor. In the long-distance limit, the cross correlations in de Sitter spacetime and the transversely accelerated vacuum decay as $L^{-2}$, whereas those in the Minkowski thermal bath decay only as $L^{-1}$. The de Sitter and transversely accelerated vacuum cross spectra coincide when $a=H$ and the separations are instantaneously matched. For a fixed experimental setup, the physical separation between the two comoving atoms in de Sitter space evolves with cosmic expansion, whereas the pulled-back cross correlations in the uniformly accelerated and thermal Minkowski configurations are stationary.
summary: This theoretical study compares the quantum correlations (cross spectra) of two atoms coupled to a scalar field in de Sitter spacetime, an accelerated vacuum, and a thermal bath. The key finding is that while the local physics can be made identical by tuning parameters, the finite separation correlations reveal distinct signatures, particularly in their spatial dependence and long-distance decay rates.
main_problem: The paper compares the two-atom cross spectra of identical two-level atoms coupled to a massless conformally coupled scalar field across three distinct physical settings: de Sitter spacetime, uniformly accelerated Minkowski vacuum, and a Minkowski thermal bath.
main_result: While the local spectra are identical under specific parameter matching ($a=H,  eta=2\pi/H$), the finite separation cross spectra differ significantly, showing distinct spatial modulation factors and different long-distance decay rates ($L^{-2}$ vs $L^{-1}$).
method: The authors derive the cross spectra by calculating the two-point Wightman function in each background and performing Fourier transforms with respect to the time difference.
model_or_system: The system involves two two-level atoms weakly coupled to a massless, conformally coupled scalar field ($\phi$). The comparisons are made in the Bunch-Davies vacuum of de Sitter spacetime, the accelerated vacuum of Minkowski space, and a thermal bath in Minkowski space.
key_observables: Two-atom cross spectra ($R^{AB}(\Omega)$), local Wightman kernels, and spatial modulation factors.
important_parameters: Local temperature parameters ($H,  eta$), separation distance ($L$), and coupling constant ($\lambda$).
main_assumptions: Weak coupling ($\lambda$ is small); the analysis relies on matching parameters like local temperature and instantaneous separation to find degeneracies.
figures_summary: The notes do not provide a summary of figures, but they detail the mathematical forms of the cross spectra in the three different backgrounds.
paper_structure: The paper proceeds by deriving the cross spectra for each of the three settings (dS, accelerated, thermal) and then comparing them, first in the zero-separation limit (local spectra) and then at finite separation, highlighting the differences in spatial dependence and long-distance decay.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant to open quantum systems and quantum optics as it explores how the environment (spacetime curvature vs. thermal bath) dictates the correlations measured by quantum probes, even when local conditions are matched.
